'''Sir Alfred Brian Pippard''' (7 September 1920 – 21 September 2008) was a British [[physicist]]. He was [[Cavendish Professor of Physics]] from 1971 to 1982, and an Honorary Fellow of [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]], of which he was the first president.

== Biography ==
Alfred Brian Pippard was born on 7 September 1920 in [[London]], the son of engineer [[Alfred John Sutton Pippard]]. He was educated at [[Clifton College]], before gaining a scholarship in 1937 to attend [[Clare College, Cambridge]], where he read physics, chemistry, physiology, and mathematics. Following the outbreak of [[World War II]], Pippard switched from chemistry to physics, due to the demand for physicists. In 1941, he graduated with [[first-class honours]] in Part II of the [[Natural Sciences Tripos]].<ref name="Royal Society">{{Cite journal | last1 = Longair | first1 = M. S. | authorlink1 = Malcolm Longair| last2 = Waldram | first2 = J. R. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2009.0014  | title = Sir Alfred Brian Pippard. 7 September 1920 -- 21 September 2008 | journal = Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society | volume = 55 | pages = 201–220 | year = 2009 | doi-access =  free}}</ref>

During World War II, Pippard worked as a scientific officer at the [[Radar Research and Development Establishment]] in [[Malvern, Worcestershire|Malvern]], where he helped develop [[microwave]] [[radar]] techniques. After the war ended, he was awarded a Stokes Studentship and returned to the [[University of Cambridge]] as a research student of [[David Shoenberg]]. He became a University Demonstrator in 1947, a University Lecturer in 1950, and a University Reader in 1959.<ref name="Royal Society"/> He was appointed [[John Humphrey Plummer Professor]] of Physics in 1960, and served as [[Cavendish Professor of Physics]] from 1971 until his retirement in 1982.<ref name="Cambridge">{{Cite web|title=Professor Sir Brian Pippard (1920 – 2008)|url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/news/professor-sir-brian-pippard-1920-2008|publisher=University of Cambridge|date=23 September 2008|access-date=2 November 2026}}</ref>

As Cavendish Professor of Physics, Pippard compiled ''Cavendish Problems in Classical Physics'',<ref>A.B. Pippard, ''Cavendish Problems in Classical Physics'' (Pamphlet) (Cambridge University Press, 1962).<br>A.B. Pippard, ''Cavendish Problems in Classical Physics'' (Pamphlet), 64 p. (Cambridge University Press, 1971)</ref> based in large part on past examination questions for Cambridge physics students.

In 1961, his graduate student [[Brian Josephson]] was working on an experimental project (the magnetic field dependence of the [[penetration depth]]), when, in his spare time, he developed a new theory of [[quantum tunnelling]] between [[superconductor]]s (now known as the [[Josephson effect]]). He submitted this work as a Fellowship dissertation to [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], and it subsequently earned him the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] in 1973.<ref name="Cambridge"/><ref>{{cite journal | last=Josephson | first=B.D. | title=Possible new effects in superconductive tunnelling | journal=Physics Letters | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=1 | issue=7 | year=1962 | issn=0031-9163 | doi=10.1016/0031-9163(62)91369-0 | pages=251–253| bibcode=1962PhL.....1..251J }}</ref>

In 1966, Pippard became the first president of the newly-founded [[Clare Hall, Cambridge]].<ref name="Cambridge"/>

== Research ==
Pippard demonstrated the reality, as opposed to the mere abstract concept, of [[Fermi surface]]s in metals by establishing the shape of the Fermi surface of [[copper]] through measuring the reflection and absorption of microwave electromagnetic radiation<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Pippard | first1 = A. B. | title = An Experimental Determination of the Fermi Surface in Copper | doi = 10.1098/rsta.1957.0023 | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 250 | issue = 979 | pages = 325–357 | year = 1957 |bibcode = 1957RSPTA.250..325P | s2cid = 120993464 }}</ref> (see the [[Skin effect#Anomalous skin effect|anomalous skin effect]]<ref>N. W. Ashcroft, and N. D. Mermin, ''Solid State Physics'' (Thompson Learning, Inc., London, 1976), Chapter 14, ''Measuring the Fermi Surface'', p. 277, ''Anomalous Skin Effect''; {{ISBN|0-03-083993-9}}. See ''[[Classical skin depth]]''.</ref>). He also introduced the notion of [[coherence length]] in [[superconductors]] in his proposal for the non-local generalisation of the [[London equations]]<ref>{{cite book|last1=Zhou|first1=Shu-Ang|title=Electrodynamic Theory of Superconductors|date=1991|publisher=Peter Peregrinus Ltd.|location=London|isbn=0-86341-257-2}}</ref><ref>F. London, ''Superfluids'', Vol. I: ''Macroscopic Theory of Superconductivity'' (Dover Publications, New York, 1961), p. 152.</ref> concerning [[electrodynamics]] in [[superfluids]] and superconductors. The non-local kernel proposed by Pippard,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Waldram | first1 = J. R. | last2 = Pippard | first2 = A. B. | last3 = Clarke | first3 = J. | doi = 10.1098/rsta.1970.0075 | title = Theory of the Current-Voltage Characteristics of SNS Junctions and other Superconducting Weak Links | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 268 | issue = 1188 | pages = 265–287 | year = 1970 |bibcode = 1970RSPTA.268..265W | s2cid = 122559890 | url = http://www.escholarship.org/uc/item/7wg0z8xs }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Pippard | first1 = A. B. | title = Quantization of Coupled Orbits in Metals II. The Two-Dimensional Network, with Special Reference to the Properties of Zinc | doi = 10.1098/rsta.1964.0008 | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 256 | issue = 1072 | pages = 317–355 | year = 1964 |bibcode = 1964RSPTA.256..317P | s2cid = 122241308 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Pippard | first1 = A. B. | title = Trapped Flux in Superconductors | doi = 10.1098/rsta.1955.0011 | journal = Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume = 248 | issue = 941 | pages = 97–129 | year = 1955 |bibcode = 1955RSPTA.248...97P | s2cid = 119893482 }}</ref> inferred on the basis of Chambers' non-local generalisation of [[Ohm's law]]) can be deduced within the framework of the [[BCS theory|BCS]] ([[John Bardeen|Bardeen]], [[Leon Cooper|Cooper]] and [[John Robert Schrieffer|Schrieffer]]) theory of superconductivity<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Bardeen | first1=J. | last2=Cooper | first2=L. N. | last3=Schrieffer | first3=J. R. | title=Theory of Superconductivity | journal=Physical Review | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=108 | issue=5 | date=1957-12-01 | issn=0031-899X | doi=10.1103/physrev.108.1175 | pages=1175–1204| bibcode=1957PhRv..108.1175B |doi-access=free}}</ref> (a comprehensive description of the details of the London–Pippard theory can be found in the book by Fetter and Walecka<ref>A.L. Fetter, and J. D. Walecka, ''Quantum Theory of Many-Particle Systems'' (Dover Publications, New York, 2003), Chapter 13, ''Superconductivity'', Section 49, ''London-Pippard Phenomenological Theory''; {{ISBN|0-486-42827-3}}</ref>).

Pippard was the author of ''Elements of Classical Thermodynamics for Advanced Students of Physics'',<ref>A. B. Pippard, ''Elements of Classical Thermodynamics for Advanced Students of Physics'' (Cambridge University Press, 1957); {{ISBN|0-521-09101-2}}.</ref>
''Dynamics of Conduction Electrons'',<ref>A. B. Pippard, ''Dynamics of Conduction Electrons'', Documents on Modern Physics (Gordon & Beach, 1965).</ref> and ''The Physics of Vibration''.<ref>A. B. Pippard, ''The Physics of Vibration'' (Cambridge University Press, 2007); {{ISBN|0-521-03333-0}}</ref> He also co-authored the three-volumes encyclopaedia ''Twentieth Century Physics''.<ref>Laurie M. Brown, [[Abraham Pais]], and Brian Pippard, ''Twentieth Century Physics'' (Institute of Physics Publishing, 1995): Vol. I; {{ISBN|0-7503-0353-0}}, 
Vol. II; {{ISBN|0-7503-0354-9}}; Vol. III; {{ISBN|0-7503-0355-7}}</ref> 

== Personal life and death ==
In 1955, Pippard married Charlotte Dyer, with whom he had three daughters.<ref name="Royal Society"/>

Pippard died on 21 September 2008 at the age of 88.<ref name="Cambridge" />
